inspired_by: Practice Test 4, Section I Part B (SAQ) - remapped to Fall 2026 CED format
directions: Section I, Part B: Short Answer. 40 minutes. This part has 3 short-answer questions and counts for 20 percent of your exam score. You must answer ALL THREE questions. There are no choices. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, which is a historian's interpretation of the past. Question 2 is based on a primary source, which is a document from the time period. Question 3 is based on a non-text source, such as an image, chart, or map. Each question has three parts, labeled A, B, and C. Answer each part in complete sentences. You do not need to write a formal essay.

stimulus.attribution: Paraphrased from Oswald Garrison Villard, John Brown 1800-1859: A Biography Fifty Years After (1910), the first full scholarly biography of Brown.
stimulus.text: Villard presented John Brown as a deeply committed antislavery militant rather than a madman. He argued that Brown's raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry in 1859 should be judged against the violence of slavery itself: Brown used force because he believed slavery was a state of war against Black people, and he had concluded that moral appeals alone would never end it.

parts: A. Briefly explain one claim Villard makes about John Brown.
B. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from the period 1848 to 1860 that supports Villard's interpretation of Brown.
C. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from the period 1848 to 1860 that challenges Villard's interpretation of Brown.
exemplar: Villard claims that Brown was a principled antislavery militant, not a fanatic, and that his violence should be measured against the violence of slavery itself.

Brown's actions in 'Bleeding Kansas,' where he led antislavery settlers in armed conflict with proslavery forces, support Villard's view that Brown was a committed militant acting on antislavery principle rather than impulse.

The failure of enslaved people to rise up during the Harpers Ferry raid challenges Villard's interpretation, because it suggests Brown badly misread the situation; Abraham Lincoln likewise judged the raid 'absurd' in an 1860 speech, arguing that even the enslaved saw it could not succeed.

stimulus.attribution: Paraphrased from the Fugitive Slave Act, passed by Congress as part of the Compromise of 1850.
stimulus.text: The law required federal marshals to arrest alleged fugitives and bring them before special commissioners. The accused person was denied a jury trial and was not permitted to testify in the hearing. Commissioners received a larger fee when they ruled that the accused person was a fugitive than when they ruled the person was free.

parts: A. Briefly explain one way the law strengthened the power of slaveholders.
B. Briefly explain one Northern reaction to the law.
C. Briefly explain how the law affected the sectional crisis of the 1850s.
exemplar: The law gave slaveholders a federal enforcement mechanism: marshals were required to help capture alleged fugitives, and commissioners had a financial incentive to rule in the slaveholder's favor.

Many Northerners who had been indifferent to abolition were outraged at being legally required to help catch fugitives, and several Northern states passed personal-liberty laws to obstruct enforcement of the act.
The law deepened sectional distrust by forcing Northerners to participate in slavery, pushing previously moderate Northerners toward antislavery politics and into the new Republican Party.

stimulus.attribution: Image 1: Jacob Riis, c.1890, public domain via Wikimedia Commons (Library of Congress). Image 2: CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.
stimulus.text: Image 1: 'Lodgers in a crowded Bayard Street tenement,' photograph by Jacob Riis, New York City, c.1890. The image shows men crowded together sleeping in a single small tenement room, with a stove and their belongings piled around them. Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Jacob_Riis%2C_Lodgers_in_a_Crowded_Bayard_Street_Tenement.jpg (Jacob Riis, c.1890; public domain via Wikimedia Commons.) Image 2: bedroom of Cornelius Vanderbilt II at The Breakers mansion, Newport, Rhode Island (mansion completed 1895). The image shows the spacious, richly furnished bedroom of a Gilded Age industrialist. Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/92/Cornelius_Bedroom_Breakers.JPG (CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.)

parts: A. Briefly describe one contrast between the two images.
B. Briefly explain one development from 1865 to 1920 that produced the living conditions shown in Image 1.
C. Briefly explain one response to the conditions shown in Image 1 during the same period.
exemplar: Image 1 shows men crowded together sleeping in a single small tenement room, while Image 2 shows a Gilded Age industrialist's spacious, elegant bedroom; the pair makes visible the gap between tenement poverty and Gilded Age wealth.
Rapid industrialization drew thousands of immigrant and rural workers into cities, where low wages and a severe shortage of affordable housing forced families into crowded, unsanitary tenements.

Settlement-house workers such as Jane Addams at Hull House, opened in Chicago in 1889, provided services to tenement neighborhoods, while Progressive reformers campaigned for tenement inspections and housing regulations.
